content: 1. Minocycline can increase the levels or effects of digoxin by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to the oral forms of both agents. Close monitoring is recommended. 2. Co-administration of minocycline and dihydroergotamine may increase the toxicity of either drug through an unknown mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. Additionally, combining ergot alkaloids and tetracyclines increases the risk of ergotism. 3. Minocycline may enhance the effects of enoxaparin through pharmacodynamic synergy. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown, but close monitoring is advised. 4. Minocycline and ergoloid mesylates may increase each other's toxicity through an unknown mechanism. Use caution and monitor closely. Co-administration of ergot alkaloids and tetracyclines increases the risk of ergotism. 5. Minocycline may decrease the levels or effects of estradiol, conjugated estrogens, estropipate, and ethinyl estradiol by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of these hormones. The risk of contraceptive failure is low, but caution and close monitoring are advised. 6. Ferric maltol, ferrous fumarate, ferrous gluconate, and ferrous sulfate can decrease the levels of minocycline by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Avoid co-administration or use alternative drugs. 7. Minocycline may increase the effects of fondaparinux and heparin through pharmacodynamic synergy. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown, but close monitoring is recommended. 8. Iron dextran complex and iron sucrose can decrease the levels of minocycline by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Avoid co-administration or use alternative drugs. 9. Isotretinoin and minocycline are contraindicated due to the risk of pseudotumor cerebri. The mechanism of this interaction is unknown. Avoid co-administration. 10. Lanthanum carbonate decreases the levels of minocycline by cation binding in the gastrointestinal tract. Administer oral tetracycline antibiotics at least 2 hours before or after lanthanum. This interaction applies only to oral tetracyclines. 11. Minocycline may decrease the levels or effects of levonorgestrel/ethinyl estradiol/ferrous bisglycinate by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of these hormones. The risk of contraceptive failure is low, but caution and close monitoring are advised. 12. Magnesium chloride, magnesium citrate, magnesium hydroxide, magnesium oxide, and magnesium sulfate can decrease the levels of minocycline by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Avoid co-administration or use alternative drugs. Administer tetracyclines at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after magnesium-containing products to avoid chelation. 13. Sodium bicarbonate and sodium citrate/citric acid can decrease the levels of minocycline by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Avoid co-administration or use alternative drugs. Separate administration by at least 2 hours. 14. Sodium picosulfate/magnesium oxide/anhydrous citric acid decreases the levels of minocycline by cation binding in the gastrointestinal tract. Administer tetracyclines at least 2 hours before and no less than 6 hours after these agents to avoid magnesium chelation. 15. Strontium ranelate decreases the levels of minocycline by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. Co-administration is contraindicated. Suspend strontium ranelate during antibiotic therapy. 16. Minocycline may increase the effects of succinylcholine through pharmacodynamic synergy, increasing the risk of respiratory depression. Avoid co-administration or use alternative drugs. 17. Sucralfate decreases the levels of minocycline by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 18. Minocycline may decrease the effects of temocillin by pharmacodynamic antagonism. Avoid co-administration or use alternative drugs. 19. Minocycline may decrease the levels or effects of thiamine by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 20. Tobramycin inhaled and minocycline both increase the risk of nephrotoxicity and/or ototoxicity. Avoid concurrent or sequential use to reduce the risk of ototoxicity. 21. Minocycline and tretinoin are contraindicated due to the risk of increased toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergy. Avoid co-administration. 22. Tripotassium dicitrato bismuthate decreases the levels of minocycline by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Avoid co-administration or use alternative drugs. 23. Minocycline decreases the effects of the typhoid vaccine live by pharmacodynamic antagonism. Co-administration is contraindicated. Wait until antibiotic therapy is complete before administering live bacterial vaccines. 24. Minocycline and valoctocogene roxaparvovec both increase the risk of hepatotoxicity. Use caution and monitor closely. Avoid combining valoctocogene roxaparvovec with other hepatotoxic agents. 25. Minocycline may increase the effects of pancuronium, rapacuronium, and rocuronium through pharmacodynamic synergy, increasing the risk of respiratory depression. Avoid co-administration or use alternative drugs. 26. Rose hips decrease the levels of minocycline by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Minocycline may also decrease the levels of rose hips by increasing elimination. The clinical significance of these interactions is unknown. 27. Minocycline may increase the effects of protamine through pharmacodynamic synergy. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 28. Minocycline may decrease the levels or effects of pyridoxine by altering intestinal flora. This interaction applies only to oral forms of both agents. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 29. Minocycline may increase the effects of methotrexate by decreasing its elimination. If tetracyclines cannot be avoided in patients receiving high-dose methotrexate, closely monitor methotrexate plasma concentrations and patients for signs and symptoms of toxicity. 30. Minocycline and methoxsalen may increase each other's toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergy, leading to additive photosensitizing effects. Use caution and monitor closely. 31. Minocycline and methoxyflurane may increase each other's toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergy, increasing the risk of nephrotoxicity. Avoid co-administration or use alternative drugs. 32. Minocycline and methyl aminolevulinate may increase each other's toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergy, leading to enhanced photosensitizing effects. Avoid co-administration or use alternative drugs. 33. Minocycline and porfimer may increase each other's toxicity through pharmacodynamic synergy, leading to enhanced photosensitivity. Use caution and monitor closely. 34. Minocycline and pretomanid may increase each other's toxicity. Pretomanid is associated with hepatotoxicity. Avoid alcohol and hepatotoxic agents, including herbal supplements and drugs other than bedaquiline and linezolid, during pretomanid therapy. 35. Minocycline may decrease the effects of penicillin G aqueous, penicillin VK, and oxacillin by pharmacodynamic antagonism. Avoid co-administration or use alternative drugs. 36. Minocycline and pexidartinib both increase the risk of hepatotoxicity. Avoid co-administration of pexidartinib with other hepatotoxic agents. 37. Minocycline may increase the effects of phenindione through pharmacodynamic synergy. The clinical significance of this interaction is unknown. 38. Minocycline may decrease the effects of piperacillin by pharmacodynamic antagonism. Use caution and monitor closely. 39. Polysaccharide iron decreases the levels of minocycline by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Avoid co-administration or use alternative drugs. 40. Trimagnesium citrate anhydrous decreases the levels of minocycline by inhibiting gastrointestinal absorption. Multivalent cation-containing products may reduce the bioavailability of tetracyclines. Administer tetracyclines at least 2 hours before or 6 hours after magnesium-containing products. Use alternatives if available.
